(2012), 'The role of family ownership in international entrepreneurship: Exploring nonlinear effects' (DOI 10.1007/s11187-010-9264-9)—which is already captured in shipped row 2322 (paired with blind target 0). The paper listed in shipped row 368—Sciascia et al. (2013), 'Family involvement in the board of directors: Effects on sales internationalization' (DOI 10.1111/j.1540-627X.2012.00373.x, online 2012)—is cited only once in Section 4.1 as background literature on the informational and experiential role of non-family directors when motivating the authors' own theoretical extension (H1). Because Sciascia et al. decisions.quote: Non-family directors are essential to facilitate the inflows and outflows of information and tangible resources. These directors, especially those who hold (or have held) important roles in other firms, provide a variety of information, knowledge, and experience crucial to identifying the risks and opportunities of entering new foreign markets (Sciascia et al., 2013 ). In this sense, we see the presence of family members on the board as a barrier to internationalization. As family directors are less likely to be able to effectively guide the FF’s expansion into international markets due to comparatively lower human and social capital relative to outside directors, stewardship considerations lead the FF to avoid internationalization when a large number of family directors sits on the board. Therefore, we hypothesize: H1: Family involvement in the board of directors is negatively related with FF internationalization.
decisions.location: Section 4.1 (Extension 1: family involvement in the board and firm internationalization)
decisions.reason: Outcomes are original-specific. Shipped row 368 refers to Sciascia et al. The paper never states what Sciascia et al. (2013) found and never compares its empirical results against Sciascia et al. (2013); the failed replication verdict applies solely to Sciascia et al. (2012) (DOI 10.1007/s11187-010-9264-9, recorded in shipped row 2322), whereas Extension 1 (H1) is the authors' own theoretical extension. Because no replication outcome for Sciascia et al. (2013) exists in the primary text, the outcome for row 368 is undeterminable.

decisions.quote: To pursue our goals of replicating and extending Sciascia et al.’s ( 2012 ) study, we followed prior replications and adopted a multi-step approach (Chandler et al., 2022 ; Ghosh et al., 2016 ). First, we directly tested Sciascia et al.’s ( 2012 ) hypothesis using a different sample, the same and two different operationalization of the dependent variable.

(2023) is a replication study that collects new multi-country survey data to re-test the curvilinear family ownership hypothesis of Sciascia et al. (2012) (DOI 10.1007/s11187-010-9264-9, captured in shipped row 2322). Both shipped and blind coding agree on record type 'replication'. Note the dependency on original: while the record itself is a replication, the specific work named in row 368 (Sciascia et al., 2013, DOI 10.1111/j.1540-627x.2012.00373.x) is only a background citation in Extension 1, which is addressed by removing row 368 on the original field.
